beats.text: Every second, software makes thousands of small decisions.
Which team should get this ticket? Is this prompt a jailbreak? How urgent is this email?
None of these are open questions. Each has a small, known set of answers, and that shape of problem deserves its own kind of model.
Meet System 1 decision engines: models that answer typed questions in a single forward pass, with a probability for every allowed answer.
Our reference implementation is Laya, an open-source, multilingual decision engine.
Today, the default is to ask a large language model.
It writes the answer one token at a time. Then your code parses the text, checks the label is one you allowed, and retries when it isn't.
A full generation, a parser and a retry path, for a decision with only three possible answers.
The name comes from Daniel Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow, which describes two modes of thought.
System 1 is fast, automatic and cheap: recognizing a face, sensing that a sentence is hostile.
System 2 is slow, deliberate and expensive: long multiplication, checking an argument.

Software has the same split. Language models made System 2 cheap enough to use everywhere, but most production decisions are still System 1 work: known options, on every request, where speed and consistency matter most.
So the fast system should answer first, and its confidence should decide when to call in the slow one.
Here's the core difference.
An autoregressive model generates its answer token by token. Each token is another sequential forward pass, and the output can be malformed, or a label you never offered.

A decision engine never writes the label. The options are part of its input. One forward pass scores every option side by side, and a softmax turns those scores into a distribution over exactly those options.
So the answer is always valid. Every option gets a probability, so you see how close the runner-up was. And the cost doesn't depend on the answer.
Every decision is expressed with three question types.
Choice picks one label from several, like which department should handle a request. The label descriptions are what the model actually matches against.
Score places the input on an ordered scale, like urgency, and returns the expected level: a probability-weighted average of the levels.
And noul returns the probability that a statement is true. Is this phishing? Does the user threaten to cancel?
Several questions about the same input are answered together, in one batched call.
Inside, each question becomes one row of tokens.
A header with the question type and instructions. Then every option, each preceded by a mask token that marks where its score will be read. Then the input itself.
The encoder is bidirectional, so each marker sees its option, the question, the rival options and the input, all at once.

But the options share one fixed token budget. With seventy-seven options, each label keeps about three tokens, and similar labels collapse into the same text. The rule of thumb: keep choice questions under about twenty options.
Now follow that row through the model.
A pretrained encoder, ModernBERT large for English, reads the whole row. A type embedding says which primitive this is, and a small two-layer decision head refines every position.
The model gathers the hidden vector at each marker, and a shared scorer turns each one into a single number: one logit per option.
Because options are inputs, not fixed output units, the same weights can score two options or twenty, even labels the model has never seen.
On a Tesla T4, one question takes about thirty-three milliseconds on the multilingual checkpoint. Ten questions take seventy-two: about seven milliseconds each.
Decoding is a few lines: divide the logits by a temperature, then apply a softmax.
Temperature never changes which option wins. It only changes how confident the model sounds.
And of the two confidence numbers the engine reports, gate on answer confidence, the probability of the chosen answer. That's the number calibration is fitted on.
For those probabilities to mean anything, honesty has to be trained in.
The tool is a strictly proper scoring rule: a reward that is maximized, on average, only by reporting what you truly believe.

If the truth is seventy percent, the log, spherical and Brier scores all peak at exactly seventy. A linear reward keeps climbing towards certainty: it pays for overconfidence. And plain accuracy can't tell fifty-one percent from ninety-nine.
Laya's training method builds on this. It's called RLCD: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.
For each item, it adds noise to the logits to sample a small group of candidate distributions, rewards each with a proper scoring rule, and compares it with its group's average.
The logits move towards the above-average samples, while a soft cross-entropy term pulls towards the teacher's full distribution, uncertainty included.

Fine-tuning is where the accuracy comes from. On the typed-decisions benchmark, the base model scores zero point three six. Fine-tuned, it reaches zero point seven seven, above the teacher's own self-agreement.
A model is calibrated when its confidence means what it says: of the answers given at eighty percent, about eighty percent are right.

The shipped checkpoints are over-confident. The fix is temperature scaling, fitted on held-out data. It never changes an answer, and it cuts calibration error from zero point four seven to zero point zero eight.
But calibration can't rescue an input the model cannot read. On Khmer, the English checkpoint scored zero accuracy, at ninety-five percent confidence.
That's why Laya ships three checkpoints and a router.
One for English, a faster multilingual one for over a hundred languages, and one fine-tuned for four specific workflows.

Before any forward pass, the router detects script and language in well under a millisecond, and sends the text to a checkpoint that can read it. Across fifty-one languages, usable coverage nearly doubles: from twenty-three to forty-five.
In production, a decision engine returns evidence, not permission.

The core pattern is confidence gating: above a threshold, act automatically; below it, escalate to a human, a rule, or a larger model. The threshold is a policy, chosen from measured accuracy and the cost of mistakes.
Roll out in stages: shadow, compare, choose a policy, then promote a bounded slice of traffic, with a rollback plan.
This matters most inside agents.
An agent loop is full of small, typed decisions. Is this input safe? Which tool comes next? Is the task done? Is this output good enough to send?
System 1 takes those in milliseconds, and hands only the uncertain cases to System 2.
In one browser agent, fine-tuning lifted the right-element choice from ten percent, which is chance, to nearly two thirds, with each step decided in about twenty milliseconds.
It isn't magic, and the limits deserve plain words.

A decision engine is not a reasoner: it can't explain itself or answer open questions. Zero-shot, the base checkpoints are near chance on specialized workflows, they ship over-confident, and long option lists or other languages need care.
So evaluate on your own traffic, fine-tune on your own decisions, fit temperatures on held-out data, and gate every change in CI.
Let System 1 answer first: in one pass, with honest probabilities.
And let calibrated confidence decide when it's time to think slow.
